chunks: "I'll describe a Cortex-M since that's most common. At the hardware level, a peripheral sets a flag and the NVIC decides this interrupt is the one to take.
The core finishes the current instruction and then automatically pushes eight registers onto the stack: R0 to R3, R12, the link register, the return address and the status register.
At the same time it fetches the handler address from the vector table, switches to handler mode, records the interrupt as active, and loads the link register with a special value called EXC RETURN.
All of that is roughly 12 cycles with no software.
Because the hardware already saved the registers a C function is allowed to trash, the ISR can be a perfectly ordinary C function.
The compiler will push the callee-saved registers if it needs them.
My code reads the data, clears the interrupt flag, and updates any shared variables, which have to be volatile and accessed atomically.
When the function returns, loading that special EXC RETURN value into the PC tells the hardware to pop the saved frame and resume the main code. On an AVR it's more manual.
The hardware only pushes the program counter and clears the global interrupt flag.
The compiler's ISR macro generates the prologue that saves the status register and every register the handler uses, then ends with a RETI.
So the same event costs more cycles, and nesting is off unless you explicitly re-enable interrupts."
